content:
(I apologise if this conversation has already been had somewhere I couldn't find, or if this belongs in a different thread - please move if so.)

Like many mathematicians, I have seen a lot of AI-generated proofs, now often accompanied with AI-generated formalisations. These make it a lot easier to verify the correctness of proof claims, but, as this crowd is well aware, this is still not perfect: e.g. if the code is just a bunch of Lean files on github, then one has to download some Lean code, run it on your machine (or some third-party code running website), understand the output (e.g. make sure there are no sorries at the most naive level, but there are also more subtle tricks, like leaving crucial steps as 'axioms', and I'm sure many others I'm unaware of). Furthermore, in these bloated many-file AI-generated formalisations, there are also often many files to trawl through, and it can be non-obvious which one is meant to represent the 'main claim'.

With AI-generated proofs/formalisations moving into the mainstream, I think there will be many mathematicians who would like to know, while learning as little Lean as possible, whether or not they should trust claims of a formalisation.

Now a lot of what is needed already exists in the Lean Live project (which is great). But I know that it is still quite overwhelming to see the full code, and hard for those unfamiliar with Lean to extract the main claim from everything else.

So maybe what I'm really asking for is simply a more user-friendly portal to Lean Live, just presenting a "main claim" view, and some newbie-friendly explanation surrounding that, saying "the proof underlying this claim does compile correctly", or "it compiles, but uses the following non-standard axioms". Together with some user-friendly way of 'expanding definitions' involved in the main claim.

Then for those who actually want to engage with the formalisation properly they can view Lean Live in the usual format, or download the files themselves, but the majority of mathematicians simply need a source they can trust saying "yes this is a correct formalised proof of this statement".

(Ideally there would also be a comment feature, so that a trusted user could comment "I have verified that this formalised statement does correspond correctly to the usual natural language statement.")

I also believe that Lean Live is not really intended for generally hosting large formalisations, so this would need to change - are there plans for expanding Lean Live in this way? (Inevitably requiring some non-trivial funding.)

You do already get something like that when you click the "Can I trust this Proof" button in the top right corner of live.lean-lang.org:

Note that while we can guarantee you that you proved the claim shown on the left hand side, we cannot guarantee that the claim as written there actually makes sense. I could also call a completely nonsensical definition InfinitudeOfPrimes and claim that I have proven it. So for this component a human will have to do.

For projects/proofs that do not fit in one live.lean-lang.org window the best solution we currently have is https://github.com/leanprover/comparator/ which is the tool that backs live.lean-lang.org, though it does take a bit of effort to set up. That being said, people have anecdotally reported that LLMs are very much capable of doing the slight amount of effort required to set it up for you.

Aha, great. So the first thing people to do is to actually use this feature and highlight their main claim as a suitable 'challenge'.

This could be made a lot more user-friendly, just with purely cosmetic changes.

Is it possible that in the near-future Lean Live could be upgraded to host larger formalisation projects also? As you say, there is only a small amount of effort involved in setting it up, but when one is faced with many AI-generated formalised proof claims, a small amount of effort (including downloading time) quickly adds up, and it would be great if this didn't need to be done separately by each curious mathematician.

So the first thing [is to make people] actually use this feature and highlight their main claim as a suitable 'challenge'.

Let me add a second wish to this list: use #formalization.yaml - indicating what you formalised, that primary source(s) you followed, if you contacted the original author beforehand, and how you formalized (purely human? AI involvement? if AI, how?). We would greatly benefit from this information becoming part of the standard for AI formalisations.
This has been discussed a couple of hours ago.

Yes, so it looks like all the hard work to create such a tool (namely comparator) has already been done, which is great. The thing to do now is to create a way for the average mathematician with no knowledge of Lean to be able to benefit from this tool.

I know that many mathematicians are immediately put off by any mention of github for example, but would still like to know whether they should trust claims of a particular formalisation or not.

A user-friendly portal to a comparator-like tool, as jargon and code-free as possible would be very useful to the wider community.

A more user friendly readme for mathematicians is surely welcome (we can have an official page in the website or something like that), but, as it has been said several time, we are talking about projects with a heavy use of AI, and the cost of asking claude or whatever to set up comparator is negligible wrt to prove a big result.

Yes, but I am not thinking of the proof creator, but their audience, who want to know if they should trust it. At the moment most proof claims I see link to a github, containing many Lean files.

I could of course say "I won't read that, set it up with comparator", but then I would have to check they have done that correctly. And the average mathematician would not know what to even ask.

So a trusted, widely known, easy to use, third party website would be very valuable.

Basically I want the proof creator to do all the work, and make the task of verification of a formalisation as painless as possible.

The people on this forum may well dramatically underestimate how much pain is involved for the average mathematician in even navigating github, let alone trying to download and run Lean themselves.

I perfectly understand, and I 100% agree that setting up challenge.lean, solution.lean and config.json is part of the job of the author (actually we are pushing very hard towards this, including formalization.yaml). So what you want to see is just a "check" or something similar that says that someone checked what the author is saying?

Note that in all cases if the final theorem cannot be stated easily with mathlib the only thing comparator, or any other tool, can say is "the author proved this complicated statement, I have no idea if what they call P=NP is what you think P=NP is".

In particular, if you are interested in someone claiming to have a proof of a big conjecture, this can go from "trusting mathlib is enough and the human check is trivial" (e.g. Riemann) to "checking the statement is really a lot of work and it has to be done by a human" (e.g P=NP).

Note that I am thinking of ways of integrating formal-conjectures tighter with comparator. Optimistically, every file in formal-conjectures could be used as a standalone challenge file. This way, mathematicians like you would be able to move the trust from individual vibeprovers to formal-conjectures authors and maintainers (including me).

What I would ideally like is a simple interface that displays just the main claim statement (together with all necessary definitions), with a 'tick' to certify that a correct proof of this statement has been uploaded.

I believe that the comparator already does basically this, so there are only two things required:
1) A nicer interface to this (purely cosmetic changes required), and
2) A centralised third-party place to host and run the required code.

The second part is the hard part, but important - otherwise we have moved the burden from 'trusting the Lean code' to 'trusting that the proof creator has accurately, and non-sneakily, implemented comparator etc'.

I know that the final burden, which is essentially unmovable, is that the curious mathematician must be able to verify that the theorem statement is correct - sometimes much easier said than done, I know. But I would like, at least, for all other barriers to be removed, leaving only this. (And even this burden could be eased via integrating with a trusted community that vouches for statements, as Yaël mentions, although this would still be limited to just those statements which appear in formal-conjectures.)

The real burden does not seem to be technical, but financial, in covering the costs of such a centralised website to host and run all this code (many of which would be quite large projects, given the typical size of an AI autoformalised proof!).
So what you want is basically a version of https://live.lean-lang.org/ (the button "Can I trust this proof?") that works for a multi file project?
Yes - if by multi file projects you mean, more generally, larger projects. (And also cosmetic changes to how that site appears to make it more user friendly, but this is a secondary concern.)
